body:
The decoder determines whether the code succeeds

Error checks return evidence about faults, not a unique correction. Different fault patterns can produce the same syndrome while changing the encoded answer differently. The decoder must choose between those possibilities to preserve the logical state.

IonQ uses Ye, Wecker, and Delfosse's beam-search decoder for the Q102 and Q66 simulations. It keeps several candidate explanations when local evidence is ambiguous. This choice is part of the quoted memory-error rates.

Distinguish detector parity from logical parity

Represent a circuit fault pattern by binary vector e. Matrix H maps it to detector parities s, while A maps it to logical-observable flips. The conditions below distinguish matching the measured syndrome from correcting the logical error. All matrix arithmetic is over \(\mathbb F_2\).

\[s=He,\quad\ell=Ae;\qquad H\hat e=s\ \text{is required, but success needs }A\hat e=Ae.\]

For independent fault probabilities \(p_j\), the most probable compatible pattern minimizes the weighted sum below. Each weight is the log-likelihood cost of choosing that fault rather than its absence.

\[w(\hat e)=\sum_j\hat e_j\log\frac{1-p_j}{p_j}\quad\text{subject to }H\hat e=s.\]

Beam search explores candidate patterns heuristically. An exact optimal quantum decoder would instead sum their probabilities within each logical equivalence class before deciding which class to correct.

Same syndrome, different logical class

A three-bit repetition example makes the ambiguity concrete. Let \(H=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(A=(1,1,1)\), and each fault probability be 0.1. Both patterns in the table produce syndrome (1,1), but their logical parities and prior probabilities differ.

Candidate\(H\hat e\)\(A\hat e\)Prior probability
010(1,1)10.081
101(1,1)00.009

The two patterns differ by 111, a logical flip. Correcting with the wrong one clears the checks but changes the encoded bit. The graph shows why both explanations fit: the middle fault flips both checks, while the two outside faults flip one each.

Belief propagation exchanges local evidence

Belief propagation exchanges evidence along this graph. A detector tells a fault variable which value would satisfy its parity, using beliefs about its other neighbors. Let D denote detector-to-fault messages, E the reverse messages, and \(\Lambda_j=\log((1-p_j)/p_j)\) the prior. The min-sum updates are given below, with \(N(i),N(j)\) denoting neighbors.

\[D_{i\to j}^{(t)}=(-1)^{s_i}\!\prod_{j'\in N(i)\setminus j}\operatorname{sign}E_{j'\to i}^{(t-1)}\;\min_{j'\in N(i)\setminus j}|E_{j'\to i}^{(t-1)}|,\qquad E_{j\to i}^{(t)}=\Lambda_j+\sum_{i'\in N(j)\setminus i}D_{i'\to j}^{(t)}.\]

A detector's confidence is limited by its least certain other neighbor. Summing incoming evidence gives \(\Lambda_j^{(t)}=\Lambda_j+\sum_iD_{i\to j}^{(t)}\), favoring no fault when positive. Loops in the graph can send conflicting evidence back around and make the beliefs oscillate.

Branch where evidence cancels

When this iteration fails, choose an unreliable unfixed variable and keep both hypotheses. Fixing \(e_j=v\) removes it and changes the remaining syndrome to \(s\oplus vH_{:j}\). Each child resumes from its parent's messages, and a beam of width B limits how many alternatives remain active.

The score below uses I iterations of belief history. Summing before taking the magnitude makes alternating positive and negative evidence count as uncertainty. The path score then ranks the retained classical search alternatives.

\[R_j=\left|\sum_{t=1}^{I}\Lambda_j^{(t)}\right|,\qquad S_{\rm path}=I^{-1}\sum_{j\ \mathrm{unfixed}}R_j.\]
Beliefs \((+8,-8,+8,-8)\) sum to zero, giving \(R_j=0\) despite their large individual magnitudes. The path score favors more consistent evidence; it is a ranking heuristic rather than a probability.

The multi-result version collects valid candidates and returns the one with least fault weight. The single-result version stops at the first valid candidate. Those stopping choices affect decoder work as well as its output.

What enters IonQ's estimate

Decoder settings affect both its search work and which faults remain uncorrected. The following settings are the ones used for the paper's memory estimate.

SettingValue
Beam width / search rounds32 / at most 10
Initial / subsequent BP iterations40 / 30 per round
Per-path iteration budget340, not total work over all paths

The paper generates Pauli-only samples with Stim and loss/leakage samples with the Walking Cat simulator. Fits of \(p_L(p)=p^5e^{a+bp+cp^2}\) extrapolate to \(9.34\times10^{-12}\) for Q102 and \(2.63\times10^{-11}\) for Q66 per SEC at \(p=10^{-4}\). Figure 7 lacks the full sample and fit-uncertainty record, and decoder timing on another code does not establish this device's latency; these remain reproduction limits.

summary: The same syndrome can come from different logical errors. Beam search retains several explanations when local evidence does not determine a correction.
